narrative.h2: A birthday video that isn't just shaky candle footage

sections.heading: Why bother with a birthday MV
sections.body: The standard birthday video is 47 seconds of someone holding a phone sideways while the room sings off-key. Useful for the moment, useless after. A scored 60-second MV cut to the guest of honor's actual favorite song travels much further — it ends up replayed on the drive home, posted on their wall the next morning, and pulled up again at the next milestone birthday as a reference point.

sections.heading: The shots that always work
sections.body: Event videographers know the canon: the candle close-up with the wish-face just before the blow, the over-the-shoulder reveal of the cake, the friends-singing wide, the gift unwrap reaction, the toast clink. The cultural touchstones are global - Marilyn Monroe's 1962 'Happy Birthday Mr. President' framing, Stevie Wonder's Happy Birthday performances for the MLK Day campaign, the viral child-cake-smash format on YouTube, Pixar's UP birthday-balloon imagery directed by Pete Docter. For milestone birthdays - 1, 18, 30, 50 - a photo-aging montage of the same person across years lands harder than any single shot, the Linklater Boyhood approach compressed to 90 seconds. Mention these moments in your prompt and Tunee assembles around them.

sections.heading: Make it the gift
sections.body: The best birthday MV isn't shown at the party — it's sent to the person three days later when the high has worn off and the texts have stopped. Tunee exports vertical for the Story, square for the post, and widescreen for the family thread, all from one render.
